> 须菩提闻说是经，深解义趣，涕泪悲泣……「是实相者，即是非相，是故如来说名实相。」……「若菩萨有我相、人相、众生相、寿者相，则非菩萨。」

In the fourteenth section the sutra's most accomplished listener breaks down and cries.

须菩提 — the one reckoned first in understanding emptiness — says he has heard nothing like this, weeps, and then makes the sharpest statement in the text: 是实相者，即是非相. What is called ultimate reality is not a mark, therefore it is called ultimate reality.

The tears matter. They are not sentimentality, and the book treats them as a warning against a common misreading of the whole path — that understanding emptiness produces coolness.

## 实相 is not a state you can look at

The formula is a guard bolted onto the word "reality" itself. Anything that can be seen, felt, attained, or described as an experience is a 相 — a mark, an object of mind.

So 实相 cannot be a particularly good meditation state. Lights, spaciousness, bliss, a sense of merging: all marks, however refined. Reality is not another, better mark. It is the absence of being pinned to any.

This is why the sutra bothers to protect the word. Every tradition eventually turns its ultimate term into an object of acquisition; the sentence removes the handle before anyone can grab it.

## 信心清净，则生实相

Belief here is not assent to a proposition. 清净 — clear, unstained — and where the belief is clear, reality is said to be born.

The causality is worth noticing: nothing is produced by effort in that clause. Clarity arises, and what was obscured appears. Like cleaning a window, not like painting one.

## 后五百岁, again

须菩提 then says: for me, hearing this and believing it is not difficult. For someone in the age after the Buddha's death — in the worst period of the timetable — to hear it and believe it, that person is rarest.

The text keeps returning to this because it is answering the reader's own excuse. The difficulty of a degraded age is being named as the condition under which the thing is still possible.

## 忍辱波罗蜜 is not endurance

Then the famous case: 歌利王 — the king who dismembered the ascetic practising patience. The sutra says that at that moment the practitioner held no mark of self, person, being, or lifespan.

忍辱 is almost always translated as patience or endurance, which produces the moral advice that one should put up with mistreatment. The book refuses this reading: 忍辱 is not swallowing an injury. It is the absence, at the moment of injury, of the two fixed positions — the one being harmed and the one doing the harm.

Two consequences follow, and they are not the same consequence:

- One may still defend oneself, refuse, leave, stop the harm. The section does not recommend passivity; the book says explicitly that stopping evil is compatible with this.
- What is gone is the injury as a possession — the item stored, replayed, and eventually repaid.

A person who leaves and holds nothing is practising 忍辱. A person who stays and stores it is not, whatever they call it.

## 无实无虚

The section's closing pair. 无实: no fixed entity. 无虚: causes and conditions do not fail.

Both together rule out the two cheap exits. "It is all empty, so nothing matters" fails the second clause. "It is all real, so everything matters absolutely" fails the first.

The working position is narrower and harder: things function completely, and none of them can be stood on.

## The test

Recall one injury you have not finished with. Not the largest — one you still carry.

Notice the mechanism: the event, then the keeping. The event is over. The keeping is the 相.

Now the harder question: what would remain of it if the "I" that was wronged were not being maintained?

That is not a rhetorical question. It is the content of the tears.
